title: How Would We Detect Extraterrestrial Life?
intro_sentence: Life elsewhere could give itself away in two ways: through the chemistry of a living world, or through the technology of a civilisation. Listening for the second has been going on since 1960.
narrative_101: There are two ways another world could tell us it is alive. Its atmosphere could carry the chemical fingerprints of life, the biosignatures that telescopes now try to read. Or its inhabitants could leave technosignatures: signs of technology, such as a radio signal no natural process makes.

The search for technosignatures is called SETI, the search for extraterrestrial intelligence. It uses the same giant radio dishes and optical telescopes that study pulsars and galaxies, and it asks a simple question of the data: is there anything here that only an engineer would make?
After more than sixty years, the answer is still no. But the search has covered only a tiny part of the sky, the frequencies and the time a signal might take, so the silence says less than it seems.
body_paragraphs: The idea that we could listen began with a 1959 paper in Nature by Giuseppe Cocconi and Philip Morrison. They suggested tuning to 1420 megahertz, the radio frequency at which hydrogen, the most common element in the universe, naturally emits, because any radio astronomer anywhere would know it. In 1960 Frank Drake tried it: Project Ozma pointed a 26-metre dish at Green Bank, West Virginia, at two nearby Sun-like stars, Tau Ceti and Epsilon Eridani.

What searches look for is a narrowband signal: radio energy squeezed into a sliver of frequency, ideally as narrow as a few hertz. Stars, pulsars and gas clouds spread their radio emission across wide bands; a transmitter concentrates it. A narrow spike in a radio spectrum is therefore the classic sign of technology, ours included. On 15 August 1977 the Big Ear radio telescope of Ohio State University recorded a strong signal, narrower than the telescope's 10-kilohertz channel, near 1420 megahertz from the direction of the constellation Sagittarius. It lasted 72 seconds, the time the target took to drift through the telescope's beam. Volunteer astronomer Jerry Ehman circled it on the printout and wrote 'Wow!'. It has never been seen again, despite many searches.

The Wow! signal shows what a real detection would need. A signal from space moves with the sky as the Earth turns, not with the telescope, while interference from phones, satellites and aircraft does not. It must repeat, so it can be studied, and a second, independent telescope must see it too. A candidate called BLC1, recorded at Parkes in Australia in 2019 while observing Proxima Centauri and reported in 2020, passed the first check, pointing on and off the star, but never reappeared; in 2021 two studies concluded it was almost certainly human-made interference. Checking, not finding, is most of the work.

Breakthrough Listen, announced in 2015 with 100 million dollars over ten years, has been among the largest of these searches, using the Green Bank Telescope and the Parkes radio telescope among others. The Allen Telescope Array in northern California, built by the SETI Institute and the University of California, Berkeley, observes for radio astronomy and SETI at the same time. China's FAST, the world's largest filled-aperture radio dish, agreed in 2016 to work with Breakthrough Listen on the search. Radio is not the only channel. Optical SETI looks for laser pulses a few billionths of a second long, brighter for that instant than a star. Infrared surveys look for the waste heat of enormous structures built around a star, an idea Freeman Dyson proposed in 1960. And as telescopes learn to read the atmospheres of other planets, industrial pollutants that nature does not make could become technosignatures too.

Carl Sagan's novel Contact, filmed in 1997 with scenes at the Very Large Array and Arecibo, imagines the moment of detection and then spends most of its story on the hard part: confirming it, and deciding what to do. Real searchers have a plan for that too. A voluntary declaration of principles, drawn up by the SETI community in 1989, says a discoverer should verify a candidate, with other observers' help, before announcing it, and should share the data openly with the scientific community. The honest state of the search: no technosignature has been found. A 2018 study estimated that all searches so far have examined a fraction of the possible signal space comparable to a hot tub of water compared with all of Earth's oceans. The silence is real, but the search has only just begun.
